chapterName: Empire: Roman Art and Architecture (c. 500 BC-AD 476)

questions.question: How did Roman portrait style shift from the Republic to the reign of Augustus?
options: From Egyptian-style profiles to frontal faces
From idealised Greek images to rugged, wrinkled realism
From full-length statues to coin portraits only
From painted panels to carved marble busts
From clay masks to bronze heads
From rugged, flaw-showing realism to idealised, Greek-flavoured images
questions.explanation: Under the Republic, showing physical flaws was a mark of good character. Augustus preferred highly idealised portraits in a Greek manner.
questions.sourceQuote: Augustus, Rome's first emperor, preferred portraits that were Greek in flavour and highly idealised.

questions.question: Which kind of Roman wall painting was later imitated by Renaissance artists?
options: Still lifes of fruit, seafood and glass jars of water
questions.explanation: Roman walls showed everyday life, animals, myths and still lifes. The still lifes caught the eye of Renaissance artists.
questions.sourceQuote: The walls show everyday life, animals, myths, erotic scenes and still lifes of fruit, seafood and glass jars of water, later imitated by Renaissance artists.

questions.question: By which routes did Greek art flood into Rome as its armies conquered the Greek world? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Greek art arrived as booty, extortion or trade. Roman temples were often decorated with secondhand Greek statues.
questions.sourceQuote: As Rome's armies conquered the Greek world, Greek art flooded into the city as war booty, extortion or trade.

questions.question: Which features marked the new style of Roman sculpture that emerged in the 3rd century AD? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Late Roman figures stressed power over beauty. Historians still debate why artists abandoned the classical style.
questions.sourceQuote: Figures became stumpy, large-eyed and rigidly frontal, stressing power over beauty.

questions.question: In the early 4th century AD, how did Rome's private houses compare in number with its apartment blocks?
options: About 45,000 town houses against 1,800 apartment blocks
About 1,800 town houses against nearly 45,000 apartment blocks
About 500 town houses against 10,000 apartment blocks
About 18,000 town houses against 4,500 apartment blocks
About 1,800 town houses against 4,500 apartment blocks
questions.explanation: Rome had 1,781 domus versus 44,850 insulae. Most city dwellers lived in these crowded blocks up to five storeys high.
questions.sourceQuote: In the early 4th century AD, Rome had 1,781 private town houses (*domus*) against 44,850 apartment blocks.

questions.question: What record did Trajan's bridge over the Danube hold?
options: First bridge built entirely of concrete
Tallest bridge of the ancient world
Longest arch bridge for a thousand years
Longest arch bridge for five centuries
First bridge to cross the Rhine
Longest arch bridge for a century
questions.explanation: Trajan's Danube bridge stayed the longest arch bridge for a thousand years. Until the Industrial Revolution, only Romans built bridges with concrete.
questions.sourceQuote: The bridge of Trajan, the soldier-emperor, over the Danube was the longest arch bridge for a thousand years.

questions.question: Why is Trajan's Column especially valuable to historians?
options: It names every sculptor who carved it
It records the founding of Constantinople
It shows the earliest known map of Rome
It lists the emperor's laws in carved inscriptions
It records real campaigns, a priceless source on Roman armour
It retells Greek myths of the Trojan War
questions.explanation: Where Greek sculptors told of war through myth, Romans preferred record. More than 2,500 figures march, build and fight on the column, like an ancient documentary film.
questions.sourceQuote: Where Greek sculptors told of war through myth, Romans preferred record, and the column is a priceless source on Roman armour.

questions.question: Where is the earliest known Roman use of concrete, dating to some time after 273 BC?
questions.explanation: Cosa was a Roman colony on the coast north of Rome. Concrete there was poured into reusable wooden frames and then faced.
questions.sourceQuote: The earliest known Roman use was at Cosa, a colony on the coast north of Rome, some time after 273 BC.

questions.question: When were domes the size of the Pantheon's finally surpassed?
options: When steel frames arrived in the late 19th century
When Gothic cathedrals rose in the Middle Ages
In the Byzantine era at Constantinople
In the 20th century with reinforced concrete
During the Renaissance, with brick domes
questions.explanation: The Pantheon's concrete dome held its record until steel frames arrived in the late 19th century. It remains the best-preserved temple of the ancient world.
questions.sourceQuote: Domes of this size were not surpassed until steel frames arrived in the late 19th century.

questions.question: When was the oldest known Roman basilica built?
questions.explanation: The oldest known basilica dates to 184 BC. Basilicas were halls where business was done and magistrates heard cases.
questions.sourceQuote: The oldest known was built in 184 BC; centuries later, Christians adopted the shape for their first great churches.
